paper_title: Generative Late-Interaction Embeddings For Visual Document Retrieval

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Late-interaction retrieval is the state-of-the-art for visual document search, but it pays for its accuracy in storage. Existing compression methods retain a subset or local average of the N~1,000 vectors per page. Under aggressive storage budgets, however, these methods degrade sharply, and alternatives require retraining the encoder. Investigating this degradation across three encoders, we found two consistent properties: the vectors lie exactly on the unit sphere and concentrate near a manifold of intrinsic dimension five to six. This geometry yields two insights. First, standard k-means centroids fall inside the sphere, causing systematic underestimation of MaxSim scores. Normalizing them to the surface is a free correction worth up to +0.093 nDCG@5 over raw centroids. Second, because the page manifold has few degrees of freedom, the full set of vectors can be regenerated from only a few. To this end, we introduce Generative Late-Interaction Embeddings (GLIE): k << N vectors per page learned from the normalized centroids to serve as both a lightweight index and a basis for regenerating the page's full embedding set. At query time, search runs exclusively on these k vectors, and a decoder expands only the top candidates back to all N vectors for exact rescoring. At four vectors per page on ViDoRe v1, GLIE retains nearly 80% of the uncompressed system's nDCG@5, against 70% for the best prior post-hoc method. These results use a 415K-parameter network fitted in under three GPU-minutes on just a thousand training pages. At a matched training budget, fine-tuning the encoder does not reach even the training-free stage of GLIE, and the full system beats it at every budget. These patterns hold across a second encoder and ViDoRe v2. By reconstructing evidence on demand rather than sampling it, GLIE opens a new axis for storage-efficient retrieval, with the decoder as its main design surface.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Retrieval over visual documents has converged on late interaction. Instead of collapsing page into one vector, models such as ColPali (Faysse et al., 2025) embed every image patch separately and score query against page with the MaxSim operator, the sum over query tokens of the maximum inner product with any page vector. This design is what makes visual retrieval work. It preserves local evidence such as table cell or phrase in figure caption, and multi-vector representations are provably more expressive than any single vector of comparable size (Jayaram, 2026). The price is storage. ColPali stores 1,031 patch vectors of dimension 128 per page, about 258 KB in bfloat16, so one million pages cost quarter terabyte of embeddings before any index structure is added. The cost is paid at rest, in memory during search, and in transfer at query time, and the community now names index footprint among the paradigms central open problems (Clavie et al., 2026). The dominant remedies compress the stored set directly: pooling merges similar vectors (Clavie et al., 2024), pruning keeps salient subset (Liu et al., 2026), merging studies combine both (Ma et al., 2025; Yan et al., 2026), and quantization stores vectors as cluster IDs and quantized residuals (Santhanam et al., 2022a). These methods share premise, that the compressed representation is subset or local average of the encoders vectors, and they also share limit. None reports operating below roughly sixteen vectors per page, and methods that reach smaller budgets retrain the encoder (MacAvaney et al., 2025; Veneroso et al., 2025; Xiao et al., 2026), which invalidates every embedding already computed. This paper starts from different question: what is the stored object, geometrically? Measuring ColPali page embeddings across all ten evaluation corpora, we find that the 1,031 vectors of page concentrate near manifold of intrinsic dimension five to six, living on the unit sphere of the 128-dimensional embedding space. Two further encoders give the same answer, one of them in 3,072-dimensional space. If page is really low-dimensional surface on the sphere, then compressed representation should describe those degrees of freedom instead of subsampling the patches. We introduce GLIE, which builds such code post hoc from frozen encoder. Per-page cluster centroids are projected back onto the unit sphere, where the encoder actually places its outputs, free correction worth up to +0.093 nDCG@5 on its own. zero-initialized network then adjusts those centroids while reading the full token set, so the code starts exactly at normalized clustering and training improves it. At query time, cheap MaxSim over the projected vectors ranks every page, and then, for the top-L candidates only, shared decoder regenerates the full set of embeddings for exact rescoring. This design shift has three structural consequences. First, the code lies on the unit sphere by construction. Second, correctness is structural: the code cannot start worse than normalized clustering, and because the decoder emits each stored vector unchanged among its outputs, regeneration can add evidence but cannot destroy it. Third, nothing in the codec conditions on corpus, so one fit serves every collection. Because what GLIE targets is the gap between compressed code and its own uncompressed system, stronger encoder raises the ceiling it is closing on, and better decoder closes more of that gap. 2 Preprint. Contributions: Geometry of the stored object. We measure page token clouds as manifold of intrinsic dimension five to six on the unit sphere. Spherical anchoring. We identify systematic MaxSim underestimate in standard k-means clustering and remove it at zero cost by re-projecting centroids to the unit sphere. Generative Late-Interaction Embeddings (GLIE). We replace extractive subset sampling with codec that stores vectors per page and regenerates all from them on demand, together with the asymmetric pipeline it enables: initial retrieval runs on the stored vectors alone, and only top-L shortlist is expanded and rescored exactly.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Late-interaction retrieval. ColBERT introduced token-level document representations scored with MaxSim (Khattab & Zaharia, 2020), ColBERTv2 compressed the index with centroid-plus-residual storage (Santhanam et al., 2022b), and ColPali transferred the paradigm to visual documents with the ViDoRe benchmark, on which late interaction dominates single-vector alternatives (Faysse et al., 2025). Video-ColBERT extends it to video and names storage as its principal drawback (Reddy et al., 2025). Jayaram (2026) proves multi-vector embeddings strictly more expressive than single vectors of comparable dimension, which cautions against collapsing pages into one vector. The gap in this line is that expressiveness is bought with storage, and no account exists of when that storage can be compressed safely. Post-hoc reduction of the stored set. Token pooling merges document vectors by hierarchical clustering, retaining about 97% of quality at pool factor 4 (Clavie et al., 2024). For visual documents, Light-ColPali finds that merging post-projector embeddings retains 97.8% of nDCG@5 at merging factor 9 and 93.6% at factor 49, roughly 41, smaller index, its most aggressive published point being about twenty-one vectors per page (Ma et al., 2025). Anchor pruning (Liu et al., 2026) and prune-then-merge (Yan et al., 2026) extend the near-lossless range. All store subset or local average of the encoders vectors, and none reports an operating point below roughly sixteen vectors per page, despite selecting, averaging, and pruning by different criteria. Section 3.1 characterizes the geometry behind that shared limit, and our method targets the budgets below it. Small budgets via retraining. ConstBERT learns projection to constant number of document vectors (MacAvaney et al., 2025), CRISP trains clusterability into the representation (Veneroso et al., 2025), and MetaEmbed trains nested meta-tokens serving budgets 1 to 64 at test time (Xiao et al., 2026). Each trains the encoder, so adopting one means giving up the public checkpoint and re-encoding the corpus. The training is substantial on its own: MetaEmbed reports 32 H100 GPUs for 30 hours. Budgets are also fixed at training time, and within that set deployed index can be truncated freely, but reaching budget outside it requires training again. Our setting is complementary: frozen public checkpoint, cached embeddings, and per-budget fit measured in GPU-minutes. Orthogonal axes. PLAID (Santhanam et al., 2022a) and EMVB (Nardini et al., 2024) compress each vector and prune candidates at query time while leaving the per-page vector count intact, Matryoshka learning shrinks the dimension axis (Kusupati et al., 2022; Xiang et al., 2026), and MUVERA sketches multi-vector scoring for candidate generation while keeping full vectors at rest (Dhulipala et al., 2024). These compose with vector-count compression. Training-free reduction is cheap and elastic but stops at shared floor. Retraining crosses the floor but gives up the frozen checkpoint. The orthogonal axes shrink bits, dimensions, or scoring cost. What none of the three asks is what the stored set actually is: low-dimensional manifold on the sphere. Section 3 measures that geometry and builds the code it implies. Table 1 summarizes.

sections.title: 3.2 WHAT A LEARNED CODE MUST ADD
sections.content: Normalized k-means is the training-free stage of GLIE, and it falls short in two ways that define the rest of the codec. First, it is blind beyond the mean. Each centroid summarizes its cluster by an average, so scoring-relevant structure inside the cluster is unrecoverable from the code no matter how the centroids are post-processed. Second, it is sample. It stores points and can only ever score with those points, so query token pointing at region the sample misses loses its evidence. code trained as description of the page can instead be expanded back into the fine token cloud when candidate matters, re-materializing evidence that no k-vector sample can hold. This is why regeneration is useful at all. GLIE discharges these requirements with three components, each of which provably starts at, and can only improve on, normalized k-means: (a) the code is initialized at it exactly, (b) is refined against 4 Preprint. the MaxSim operator itself while reading the full token set, and (c) is decoded under guarantee that regeneration never lowers stored score. The encoder is frozen throughout and everything happens post hoc on cached embeddings. Figure 2 shows the fitting procedure and Figure 3 the query path.

sections.title: 3.3 SPHERICAL ANCHORING
sections.content: Per page, k-means centroids of the token set are computed and projected onto the unit sphere, uj = cj/cj. By Proposition 1 the projection removes systematic MaxSim underestimate at zero cost. Empirically it is worth +0.031 to +0.093 nDCG@5 on the full benchmark, shrinking as grows exactly as the proposition predicts  (Table 7)  . Normalized clustering is therefore the training-free stage of GLIE and the floor every learned component must clear, as well as the practical one-line recommendation for any dot-product late-interaction system that clusters: normalize your centroids.

sections.title: 3.4 ZERO-INITIALIZED REFINEMENT THAT READS THE PAGE
sections.content: Defining = {u1, . . . , uk} for the anchors, shared cross-attention module refines them against the full token set, with as queries and as keys and values, = normalize(cid:0)U + πθ(Attn(U, X, X))(cid:1), where Attn(Q, K, ) is multi-head attention, normalize projects each row back to the unit sphere as in Section 3.1, and the output projection πθ is initialized at zero, so at initialization πθ() = 0 and = exactly. Intuitively, the code begins exactly at normalized clustering and training can only move it where the objective improves, so the strongest training-free solution is the floor rather than competitor. The correction reads directly, so the code can encode scoring-relevant structure that centroids average away, which no post-processing of the centroids alone could recover. The refiner and decoder together hold 415K parameters against the 3B backbone and run once per page at indexing time. (2)

sections.title: 3.5 ANCHORED GENERATIVE READ-OUT
sections.content: A shared decoder gψ expands the stored vectors back into unit vectors for reranking. Its structure encodes three guarantees. First, count-proportional slots: cluster owns nj output slots, so the decoder reproduces the pages actual cluster structure rather than fixed learned layout. Second, an exact anchor: slot 0 of each cluster emits the refined vector verbatim, so the decoded set contains the code set, and because MaxSim is maximum, MaxSim(Q, gψ(C)) MaxSim(Q, C) per query token. Intuitively, regeneration can add evidence but structurally cannot destroy it, with no tuning. Third, bounded displacement. Each generated child starts at its clusters anchor and moves along the surface of the sphere, never toward or away from the center, by learned step of at most α = 0.75, then renormalized. child can therefore sit at most arctan(0.75) 37 from its anchor, so clusters children fill patch around it rather than scattering across the sphere. Which child is which is encoded by its position in the cluster with fixed sine and cosine features, so no per-slot parameters are learned and one decoder serves clusters of any size. Prior compression selects or averages among the encoders vectors at indexing time, and that fixed set is all query can ever be scored against. The generative read-out instead re-materializes the fine structure only when candidate is worth the cost.

sections.title: 3.6 TWO-STAGE INFERENCE
sections.content: GLIE (Figure 3) combines the code and the read-out: 1. Stage 1 (retrieve): score every page against the query by MaxSim over its stored vectors, at the cost of pooled baseline. 2. Stage 2 (regenerate and rerank): expand the top-L candidates (L = 20) back to vectors with gψ and rescore them by full MaxSim. Non-candidates keep their first-stage order. The asymmetry is the point: cheap over everything, expensive over almost nothing. Preprint. Figure 2: Training. The encoder stays frozen. The projection is initialized at normalized k-means and refiner adjusts it from there. Five kinds of loss jointly optimize the projected and regenerated vectors, with the MaxSim and listwise terms applied to both. Figure 3: Inference. Every page is scored on its projected vectors, then only the top-L shortlist is decoded back to full length and rescored exactly.

sections.title: 3.7 TRAINING
sections.content: Two objects are trained and each has one job. The code is scored against every page, so it must rank. The regenerated set is scored only on the shortlist, so it must rank and it must be page. The losses follow from those two jobs. The code must retrieve. Two things make code retrieve like the full page. Firstly, every query token should find in the code the same best match it finds in the page, so we match per-query-token 6 Preprint. MaxSim values against the frozen encoder, Ltok = 1 (cid:88) (cid:16) j=1 max qj, ˆxl max (cid:17)2 qj, xi . (3) Here xi ranges over the pages encoder vectors and ˆxl over the vectors of the read-out being trained, the code vectors for the code and the regenerated vectors for the decoder, so the same term applies to both. Secondly, the order of candidate pages should be the teachers, so listwise KL over each querys candidate list matches the ranking and not only the scores. Together these make the code drop-in first-stage index. The regenerated set must retrieve, and it must be page. The same two terms apply to the regenerated vectors, since they are what the shortlist is rescored with. Three more terms enforce what set of vectors must be to stand in for the real one. It must not invent evidence. Section 3.1 showed that normalized code can overestimate, and regenerated page that scores non-relevant candidate above its true MaxSim is exactly the error that breaks rerank, so one-sided penalty charges negatives only when they exceed the teacher. It must have the right shape. Each clusters children should occupy the region its real patches occupy, in no particular order, which Chamfer distance within each cluster of the relevant page measures. And it must reach as far as the real page in every direction. MaxSim reads the extreme point of the set along the query, so we match the support function, the farthest extent of the set along fixed bank of random directions, between the regenerated and real vectors of the relevant page. Reconstruction error is absent on purpose. It is minimized by placing every child near its cluster mean, which is exactly the collapse that loses the extreme points MaxSim reads.

sections.title: 4.1 SETUP
sections.content: Protocol. We evaluate on all ten ViDoRe v1 subsets (Faysse et al., 2025) under the benchmarks standard protocol. The codec is fitted once on 5,000 pages of the public ColPali training collection, and applied frozen to every test subset. The corpus of each subset is its set of unique pages, deduplicated by image identity, with query-less pages kept as distractors. We report single-relevant nDCG@5. Frozen ColPali v1.3 is used, which gives 1,031 patch vectors of dimension 128 per page. Budgets {2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64}, i.e. 516 down to 16 fewer stored vectors. Section 4.2 repeats the sweep on ViDoRe v2 (Mace et al., 2025) and Section 4.6 on ColQwen2. Baselines. All post hoc on the same frozen encoder at identical stored budget: raw per-page kmeans, semantic cluster merging (the training-free stage of Light-ColPali (Ma et al., 2025), with its fine-tuning removed), and sequential token pooling (Clavie et al., 2024). Margins are always reported against the strongest training-free baseline chosen per subset and per budget. We additionally reproduce Light-ColPalis fine-tuning stage at matched training budget and source (Section 4.4). Learned rows are means over three training seeds. Architecture, optimization, and evaluation details are in Appendices and B.

sections.title: 4.2 MAIN RESULTS: VIDORE V1 AND V2
sections.content: Aggressive-budget results. GLIE reaches 79% of uncompressed retrieval quality storing 1.0 KB per page and 91% at 4 KB, and beats every prior baseline on all subsets of both ViDoRe v1 and v2 at every budget (Table 3, 4). The best-powered subset is also among the strongest. TAT-DQA, with 1,663 queries, shows margins +0.039 to +0.054 at 8. Where the gains sit. The margin is positive at every budget but not uniform, and its profile differs between the two benchmarks (Figure 1). On v1 it forms plateau of about 0.04 across 8, halves at = 16, and decays to noise by = 32, mean of +0.039 below = 8 against +0.010 above. The stored code alone turns slightly negative at = 64, where normalized clustering already sits 0.027 from the ceiling and refiner fitted elsewhere has nothing left to correct. Four of the ten v1 subsets have ceilings of 0.94 to 0.98, so part of that high-budget decay is saturation rather than method failure. On v2, which saturates nowhere, the margin never decays and the band the read-out 7 Preprint. sections.title: 4.3 WHAT LIMITS THE CASCADE
sections.content: The oracle row splits the residual error (Figure 4). At = 4 on v1 the gap from GLIE to the oracle, 0.657 to 0.782, is decode fidelity, recoverable by better decoding, while the gap from the oracle to the ceiling, 0.782 to 0.836, is shortlist recall, recoverable only with larger L. Widening the shortlist confirms the split: from = 5 to = 100 the oracle rises from 0.705 to 0.822 while GLIE moves only from 0.647 to 0.660, so the shortlist is not the binding constraint and = 20 is already past the point of diminishing returns. The generative read-out contributes +0.013 to +0.016 at = 4 to 8, third of the total margin at near-zero marginal cost, and further +0.13 sits in the same shortlist waiting on better decoder. On v2 that decode-fidelity term stays large at every budget, which is why the read-out keeps earning there. Decoding is therefore the lever with measured headroom, since refining the code further is bounded by what vectors can hold. Figure 4: Decomposition of the gap to the uncompressed ceiling at each budget on ViDoRe v1. 8 Preprint.

sections.title: 4.4 A SMALL CODEC BEATS FINE-TUNING AT A MATCHED BUDGET
sections.content: Fine-tuning the encoder on 4,000 pages does not reach free normalized clustering at any budget in our hands  (Table 5)  , while the same source and budget spent on frozen-backbone codec beats it at all six, by +0.074 to +0.132. The gap is not evidence against Light-ColPali, whose authors train on 130K queries for about 72 GPU-hours per budget. Instead, it measures what small training budget buys: 13.3M LoRA parameters over 1.5 GPU-hours perturb 3B backbone too little to help and enough to hurt, whereas 415K parameters over under three GPU-minutes reshape the stored code directly. Appendix gives the adapter, merge, and training settings of the reproduction. sections.title: 4.5 STORAGE & DATA EFFICIENCY
sections.content: Storage at = 4 is 1,040 bytes per page against 257.8 KB uncompressed, so one million pages shrink from 258 GB to 1.0 GB. Because the backbone is frozen, changing the storage budget of deployed index touches only cached embeddings, while fine-tuned method must re-encode the corpus. Refitting on 1,250, 2,500, and 5,000 source pages leaves the margins statistically unchanged (+0.048/ + 0.052/ + 0.049 at = 4), so it saturates on roughly thousand pages, hundred times smaller slice of the collection than the encoder trains on. More data is not the lever. What the codec learns is property of the encoders geometry, which Table 2 showed is corpus-independent.

sections.title: 4.6 THE RECIPE TRANSFERS TO A SECOND ENCODER
sections.content: On ColQwen2 the codec retains 82% of uncompressed quality at = 4  (Table 6)  . Against spherical anchoring alone, which already reaches 0.702 at = 4 on this encoder, it wins at five of six budgets and loses only at = 2. ColQwen2 is the stronger encoder, so clustering already sits closer to its ceiling at every budget and the room learned code has is correspondingly smaller and flatter, with margins of +0.015 below = 8 against +0.013 above. Read together with ViDoRe v2  (Table 4)  , which saturates nowhere and keeps its margins to = 64, this shows that how sharply the gains concentrate at aggressive budgets is property of the setting rather than constant. sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: Late-interaction retrieval owes its accuracy to storing token-level vectors and its cost to the same decision. We argued the way out is geometric. pages thousand token vectors concentrate near manifold of intrinsic dimension five to six on the unit sphere, the same on every corpus and all three encoders we measure. The sphere yields free correction any dot-product late-interaction system can adopt today. The small dimension is what makes the method possible, since page with few degrees of freedom can be carried by few anchors and one shared decoder, which is why 415K parameters and thousand training pages suffice. We read the result as opening new axis for the storage problem rather than closing it. Generating on demand is different lever from storing fewer or smaller vectors, and the shortlist oracle measures how much of it is still available: at four vectors per page, decoding the same code and the same shortlist perfectly would reach 0.782 against our 0.657. Better decoders are therefore the immediate move on this axis, and the code itself is bounded by what vectors can hold. Three next steps look most promising. Extending the sweep to further late-interaction encoders would test how far the recipe carries beyond the two we evaluate. Composing GLIE with quantized storage, since the two act on different axes of the footprint. And the largest gains should wait where token sets are largest and most redundant, which points to video late interaction (Reddy et al., 2025).

sections.title: A IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS
sections.content: Architecture. The refiner is one four-head cross-attention layer with zero-initialized output projection. The decoder is two-layer MLP of width 256 with the bounded step of Section 3 capped at α = 0.75. Together they hold 415K parameters. Per-page k-means uses two restarts. Optimization. We train with AdamW at learning rate 2 104 and weight decay 104, cosine decay to 5% of the initial rate over 100 epochs, and gradient clipping at 1.0. batch is eight queries, each paired with its relevant page and seven hard negatives drawn from the fifty highest-scoring non-relevant pages under the frozen code. Loss weights are 1.0 for the MaxSim and listwise terms on the regenerated set, 0.5 for the same two terms on the code, 0.5 for the Chamfer and overshoot terms, and 0.1 for the support term, with listwise temperature of 0.07, 128 fixed support directions, and 48 sampled patches per cluster for the Chamfer term. Model selection and inference. Two checkpoints are kept from each run, the best single-stage code and the best cascade on that holdout, and each is reported on the metric it is deployed under. The shortlist is = 20 and pages outside it keep their first-stage order. Stored vectors are bfloat16 with one fp16 norm and one uint16 count per cluster. One budget fits in 2.7 minutes on single NVIDIA A100 80GB, and seeds are 0, 1, and 2.

sections.title: B EVALUATION PROTOCOL DETAILS
sections.content: No learned component ever sees ViDoRe test query or page, so we evaluate on all queries of each subset: 3,943 queries in total, of which 1,663 are on TAT-DQA. The corpus of each subset is its set of unique pages, de-duplicated by image identity, with query-less pages kept as distractors. Our pipeline reproduces the official leaderboard average for ColPali v1.3. Margins are reported against the strongest training-free baseline chosen per subset and per budget. Learned rows are means over three training seeds with seed standard error at most 0.002 on every cell and margin. LIGHT-COLPALI REPRODUCTION Light-ColPali (Ma et al., 2025) merges post-projector embeddings by clustering and fine-tunes the encoder through the merge. We reproduce the fine-tuning half on the same source as GLIE. The merge follows the authors: per-page cluster assignment is computed without gradient, and the cluster means are renormalized and trained end to end. Because vidore/colpali-v1.3 is itself PEFT checkpoint, we merge and unload its own adapter before attaching fresh LoRA (rank 32, α = 32, dropout 0.05). We verify at initialization that the untrained merge scores exactly as stock ColPali plus merging before any update. Training uses the pairwise loss of the ColPali training recipe at batch 8 with gradient accumulation 4, five epochs over 4,000 query-page pairs and 10% warmup. One adapter is trained per budget, 13.3M trainable parameters and about 1.5 GPU-hours each on one A100, and evaluated zero-shot on all queries of the ten ViDoRe v1 subsets under the same protocol as GLIE. The published method trains on 130K queries for about 72 GPU-hours per budget and reports results only at 16, so Table 5 is statement about what matched small budget buys and not about the published method.
